parts.title: The worst tour guide
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
On our family holiday in Italy, we booked a day tour of an old town. We had read good reviews, and my mother was looking forward to it for weeks. But from the first minute, we could see that our guide, a young man called Dario, had a problem.

He spoke so quietly that nobody at the back could hear him. When he pointed at a building, he often said, "I think this was a church... or perhaps a school." At one point, he took us to a beautiful square and told us that it was built in the twelfth century. A lady in our group, who was a historian, politely said that it was built in the sixteenth.

Then it began to rain. Dario had no umbrella, and he walked so fast that we nearly lost him twice. Finally, he stopped at a cafe and said that this was the end of the tour. We had paid fifty euros each!

However, there was a happy ending. The cafe owner, who had heard everything, brought us free coffee and gave us a map with all the sights marked. We spent the afternoon on our own, and it was the best part of the day.

questions.explanation: He spoke so quietly that people could not hear him.

questions.explanation: She politely said the square was built in the sixteenth century.

questions.explanation: Dario stopped at a cafe and said the tour was over.

parts.title: The history of souvenirs
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
People have always brought things home from their travels. [1] Pilgrims in the Middle Ages, for example, took small badges from holy places to show that they had been there.

In the eighteenth century, rich young Europeans toured Italy and France. [2] They bought paintings, statues and books, and sent them back by ship.

When railways and cheaper hotels arrived, ordinary people could travel too. [3] Their shops sold small, cheap objects with the name of the town on them.

Postcards became very popular in the twentieth century. [4] A simple picture and a few words could tell friends that you were thinking of them.

Today, many souvenirs are made in distant factories. [5] The best ones, however, are still made by local people using traditional skills.
sentences: Seaside towns soon filled with gift shops.
These are often cheaper but less special.
The idea was to prove that you had really been there.
Most of them travelled for many months.
Most of these cost more than a week's wages.
Hotels sometimes give a small gift to their guests.
They were easy to buy, light and quick to send.
Visitors often prefer to buy food.

gaps.explanation: The idea was to prove you had been there; the next sentence gives pilgrims and badges.
Most of them travelled for many months; the next sentence says what they bought.
Seaside towns filled with gift shops; the next sentence says their shops sold cheap objects.
They were easy to buy, light and quick to send; the next sentence says a simple picture could tell friends.
These are cheaper but less special; the next sentence says the best are made by local people.

parts.title: Choosing a souvenir
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Choosing a souvenir can be harder than it seems. Many tourists buy the first thing they see, [1] later they regret it. Before you spend any money, walk around the market and compare the prices. [2] you find something you like, ask where it was made. Real handmade objects are often more expensive, but they last longer. Remember that you have to carry everything home, [3] be careful not to buy something heavy or fragile. A good tip is to choose an object that reminds you of a special moment. It can be anything: a stone from the beach, a ticket, or [4] a simple postcard. Do not forget the rules about taking food or plants through customs, because some countries do not allow [5]. Finally, if you are buying a gift, think about the person who will [6] it.

gaps.explanation: And joins two actions: they buy something and regret it later.
When you find something you like, ask where it was made.
So gives a result: you have to carry everything, so be careful.
Even/just a simple postcard shows that it does not have to be special.
Do not allow it: object pronoun after the verb.
The person who will receive it.

parts.title: A message from a tourist office
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: clerk
turns.text: Hello, and thank you for calling the Seaview Tourist Office. We are open from nine to five every day, except Sunday, when we are closed. On Saturdays we close early, at one o’clock. This week, we are offering a special trip to Gull Island, and I’d like to tell you about it. The boat trip takes about three hours, including one hour on the island. Many people think that it takes only an hour, because the island looks so close, but the sea is rough around the rocks, so the boat goes slowly. Now, the prices. An adult ticket costs eighteen pounds, and a child ticket costs twelve. Students pay fifteen with their card. You can buy them here in the office or on our website. The boat leaves from the harbour at ten past ten. It doesn’t leave from the beach, as some visitors think, and it doesn’t leave from the station either. Please arrive twenty minutes early, because we count everybody before we go. We also have the cliff tour, which is on Wednesday morning at nine. There is another one on Thursday afternoon, but it’s full already. Our guide has worked here for twenty years and he knows every bird. Now, what to bring. The weather here changes quickly, so even if it’s sunny when you leave, you should bring a raincoat. A hat and sun cream are useful too, but you can buy those at the harbour shop. Finally, if the sea is too rough, we will cancel the trip, and you will get your money back. We’ll send you a message at eight, so please check your phone. Thank you for calling, and we look forward to seeing you.

gaps.prompt: The tourist office does not open on ___
gaps.explanation: It is open every day except Sunday; on Saturdays it only closes early.

gaps.prompt: The journey to the island takes about ___ hours
gaps.explanation: It looks like one hour, but the boat goes slowly; the trip takes about three hours.

gaps.prompt: A ticket for a grown-up costs ___ pounds
gaps.explanation: A child ticket is twelve and a student ticket fifteen; the adult price is eighteen.
The boat does not leave from the beach or the station but from the harbour.

gaps.prompt: The walk along the cliffs is on ___ morning
gaps.explanation: The Thursday tour is in the afternoon and it is full; the cliff tour is on Wednesday morning.

gaps.prompt: Because of the changeable weather, visitors should bring a ___
gaps.explanation: A hat and sun cream can be bought at the harbour shop, but visitors must bring a raincoat.

parts.title: An interview with a tour guide
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Beck, how did you become a tour guide?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: By accident, to be honest. I didn’t answer an advert, and I never studied history, I trained as a chef, and I thought I would work in a restaurant forever. A friend of mine had a group of tourists one day and he was ill, so he asked me to take them round the old town. I was terrified, but they loved it, and I never went back to the kitchen.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What does a good guide need?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: People think a university degree, or a fast car, but a guide walks most of the time. What you really need is patience and a sense of humour. Some visitors ask the same question five times, and you have to smile every time.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Why is the work never boring?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: The routes are almost always the same, and the weather in this city is lovely, so that isn’t it. What changes is the people. Every group is different. I’ve had singers, football fans and a group of retired judges. They all notice different things, and I learn something new each time.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What was the strangest question a visitor has asked you?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Oh, the toilet and the ticket price I hear ten times a day, those are normal. The strangest was from a woman who asked if the castle had a swimming pool. She’d read about a royal bath in a book. I tried not to laugh, and I said that the king was a very clean man.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do tourists get wrong?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: They try to see everything in one day. They have a list, and they run from the cathedral to the museum to the castle, and by six in the evening they are exhausted. They don’t wake up late, in fact, many get up too early. I always tell them to choose three places and to enjoy them.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you suggest for somebody in a new city?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: A taxi tour is quick, and staying in the hotel is safe, but you don’t learn much. Take a map, walk without hurrying, and talk to the people who live there. Ask the baker where he eats, or the old man on the bench what has changed. That’s how I learned my own city, and I’m still learning it after twenty years. There’s always one more street that I don’t know, and one more story behind a door.

questions.prompt: How did Beck become a guide?
questions.explanation: He did not answer an advert or study history; a sick friend asked him to take a group round the old town.

questions.prompt: What does a good guide need?
questions.explanation: A guide walks most of the time and does not need a degree or a car; patience and a sense of humour are the key.

questions.prompt: Why is the work never boring?
questions.explanation: The routes are the same and the weather is nice, but every group of people is different.

parts.instructions: Answer the questions. Try to give a reason or an example with each answer.

questions.prompt: Why do tourists like to buy souvenirs?
Is it better to travel alone or with a tour group? Why?
